findings.title: Comm scale contradiction
findings.description: Engaging communication is defined in Measures as the mean of four items each scored 1-4, so the composite cannot exceed 4. Results describes the same measure as lying on a '1.25-5 scale'. Verified verbatim in the source PDF (pages 5 and 6), so this is not a markdown-extraction artifact. Both stated bounds come from the paper itself (rulebook rule 4: a stated constraint, not an assumed one). The most economical reading is that 1.25-5 is the OBSERVED range and the upper value is a typo for 4 (1.25 = 5/4 is exactly attainable for a four-item 1-4 mean, which supports the observed-range reading). Note also the interpretive gloss is internally odd: on the 1-4 scale 3.83 sits close to 'Outstanding'

Results describes the same measure as lying on a '1.25-5 scale'. Verified verbatim in the source PDF (pages 5 and 6), so this is not a markdown-extraction artifact. Both stated bounds come from the paper itself (rulebook rule 4: a stated constraint, not an assumed one). The most economical reading is that 1.25-5 is the OBSERVED range and the upper value is a typo for 4 (1.25 = 5/4 is exactly attainable for a four-item 1-4 mean, which supports the observed-range reading). Note also the interpretive gloss is internally odd: on the 1-4 scale 3.83 sits close to 'Outstanding' (4), not 'good' (3) as the sentence states. Dispersion is compatible with either reading, so nothing here is impossible; it is a definitional inconsistency that warrants correction because it changes how a reader interprets the reported effect per one-unit increase.

findings.description: The printed coefficient and SE imply p = 0.0013, and even the most favourable corner of the rounding intervals gives 0.0012 -- above the printed '<.001'. findings.title: T3 idm p rounding
findings.description: The recomputed p is 0.0047, which at the two-decimal precision used throughout the table would print as .00, not .01. This is the paper's second-strongest headline result, so it is worth recording, but the direction is CONSERVATIVE -- the printed p overstates rather than understates the p-value, which is the opposite of the pattern that motivates concern. A benign explanation is that the authors rounded up rather than print '.00'; note however that the same table does print a bare '0' elsewhere, so the convention is not applied consistently.

findings.description: A p-value printed as exactly '0' is not a possible value for a probability; the correct rendering is a bound such as '<.001', which the very same row uses in the adjacent model. Recorded because it is the kind of inconsistency that indicates the table was assembled by hand.

findings.title: T3 baseline precision uninformative
findings.description: Recorded explicitly as a NON-finding to prevent a false accusation. At the printed precision (coefficient to 2 dp, SE to 3 dp) the rounding intervals admit z anywhere from 2 to 10, so the achievable p spans roughly 0.046 down to 1e-23. The printed .01 sits comfortably inside that interval. The tool returns `p_matches: false` and severity `suspicious` when handed the point values, but that verdict is an artifact of precision-blind comparison: this statistic is UNINFORMATIVE, not inconsistent. The same reasoning applies to the '<.001' in model 3 of this row.

findings.description: Denominator matters: 59 of 63 coefficient/SE/p triples reproduce their printed p-value to the displayed precision. findings.title: Sprite zerocount vs any ebp INCONCLUSIVE
findings.description: DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED AS A FINDING. '38 (59%) use at least one EBP' implies exactly 26 coalitions with a count of zero. The Python SPRITE sampler produced 36-38 zeros in every one of 300 reconstructions, which would suggest the two rows cannot coexist. But the cross-check against rsprite2 returned valid distributions with markedly fewer zeros, so the two engines disagree about which zero-counts are attainable. Per the tooling rule, engine disagreement is a bug in our instrumentation, not evidence about the paper, so no anomaly is claimed here. This would have been a false accusation without the cross-check. A reader with the raw data could settle it; recorded so the question is visible r

findings.title: Duplication across tables
findings.description: No improbable cross-independent-source overlap: the tool reports zero identical pairs between blocks that do not share a sample_id. The four exact repeats are all within a single table, between models that differ only in which leadership predictor is included and that share the same covariates and the same coalitions -- near-identical covariate estimates there are expected, not anomalous, and the tool scores them `consistent`. The eight 'digit_transposition' near-matches are coincidences among small two-digit values (0.1 vs 0.01) across tables with different outcomes and different scales; they carry no signal.

findings.notes: The paper's third headline claim -- carried in the abstract, the discussion and the conclusion -- is a null result, and it is stated as an absence of association rather than as a failure to detect one. It cannot be evaluated with the tooling because no interval is reported and no smallest effect size of interest is stated, so the largest fidelity effect the data still permit is not recoverable from the published numbers. What IS visible on the face of Table 4 is that the standard errors (0.60, 0.98, 0.72) are large relative to a 1-7 outcome scale, and that the fidelity analysis rests on 35 of the 64 coalitions. Recording this as indeterminate rather than as a pass: 'not significant' has been reported as 'not associated', and the paper supplies nothing that would let a reader distinguish the two. The paper's own framing is more careful in one place -- 'It is not yet clear how inclusive leadership improves evidence-based practice fidelity' -- than in the abstract.

findings.title: Multiplicity uncorrected (Tables 2-4; Results para 3)
findings.description: Nine primary tests are reported across three correlated outcomes and three highly correlated predictors, with no correction described and none of the six positive results stronger than p = .01. The three predictors are facets of a single construct measured on the same member survey, and the three outcomes are all functions of the same coalitions' EBP portfolios, so the tests are far from independent -- which cuts both ways, making a simple Bonferroni too harsh but leaving the nominal p-values optimistic. Flagged for the editorial stage to weigh against the paper's appropriately hedged language ('may promote'), which is more cautious than the abstract's flat 'was positively associated'.

findings.title: Table header mislabelled (Tables 2, 3 and 4, column sub-headers)
findings.description: All three regression tables label their estimate columns 'M (SD)' -- mean and standard deviation -- under a group header reading 'Coefficient', and the footnote reinforces the error by glossing SD as 'standard deviation'. The parenthetical values are standard ERRORS, as confirmed by the fact that b/SE reproduces the printed p-value in 59 of 63 cells. Confirmed verbatim in the PDF, so this is the published text and not an extraction artifact. Recorded because it is a genuine hazard to readers and to any downstream meta-analysis, which would otherwise pool these as dispersion rather than precision; it also means Table 1 and Tables 2-4 use the same notation for two different quantities.
